title: Tataka's forest
hookLine: a forest that used to be farmland, and the story of who emptied it

cards: The three travelers cross the Ganga where the Sarayu pours into it, and Rama hears the roar of the two rivers meeting. On the far side, the land changes. A dark, thick forest.
No paths. Crickets, harsh birdcalls, lions, tigers, boars, elephants. Nobody lives here.
What is this place, Rama asks. The sage's answer surprises him. Not long ago, these were two rich farming lands, full of people and harvests.

teach.b: Her name is Tataka. She was born a yakshi, a nature spirit, daughter of a yaksha named Suketu, who prayed for a child and was given a daughter with the strength of a thousand elephants.
She married Sunda and had a son, Maricha: the same Maricha who has been ruining Vishvamitra's sacrifice.
When her husband died, Tataka and her son attacked the great sage Agastya, and Agastya cursed them both. Maricha became a rakshasa.
Tataka became a terrible devourer, and since then she has turned this whole country into wilderness. She has to be stopped, the sage says. By you.
Rama stops. Valmiki lets him ask a real question: she's a woman; how can a woman have such strength? The sage, knowing what Rama is really asking, makes his case before Rama acts.
A protector has a duty. When anyone, man or woman, is destroying the lives of others, the protector cannot step back. It's a hard teaching, and the text doesn't hide that it's hard.
But notice what Valmiki honors first: the question. Hindu learning has always run on questions. The Upanishads are mostly conversations, a student asking, a teacher answering.
And the Bhagavad Gita says the way to learn is by bowing to the teacher, by asking, and by serving.
Rama does all three. He trusts his guru enough to ask, and his guru respects him enough to answer before asking him to act. Tomorrow, what he decides.

how: Tataka's story is told in Ramayana recitations and in Ramlila performances as the young Rama's first test; some teachers pause on Rama's question and Vishvamitra's answer, since Hindu learning has long been carried on by question and answer between student and guru.

o: a river goddess where the Ganga and Sarayu meet
a sage's wife who lives hidden in the forest
a yakshi, cursed by Agastya, who emptied two rich lands

s: the forest had always been wild
the sage says it was once rich farmland, emptied by Tataka.
the same rakshasa who has been ruining Vishvamitra's sacrifice.
in Hindu learning, questioning your teacher is disrespectful
the Gita says learn by bowing, by asking and by serving. Rama asks first, and the sage answers before he acts.

games.q: you're Rama, first time outside the walls. a sage asks you to stop a yakshi who has emptied two lands. what do you do first?
games.why: he asks how a woman can be so strong, and Vishvamitra answers before Rama decides. a guru who answers, a student who asks: that's how Hindu learning works.

practice: Five hundred days; let that land for a breath. Then bring one real question to the sit: something about God, your path, or a teaching that has never sat right with you. Don't rush to answer it.
Hold it honestly, the way Rama held his before he acted. If you pray, offer the question itself as the prayer. If you don't, just let it be asked.
In this tradition, asking is part of the path.

wordCard.voice: Tataka. The yakshi, cursed by Agastya, who turned two rich lands into wilderness, and whom Vishvamitra asks Rama to stop, after Rama asks his question.

orig.note: Sanskrit tāṭakā: the yakshi of the forest, cursed by Agastya.

carryVoice: Your line: ask the guru, then act. Rama questioned first, and his teacher answered. Day five hundred, and counting.
